newsitem.title: UK: Airbus eyes McDonnell Douglas' Europe market share.
newsitem.headline: Airbus eyes McDonnell Douglas' Europe market share.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
Airbus Industrie will be hoping to win the lion's share of orders worth upwards of $8 billion as European airlines replace about 160 McDonnell Douglas jets over the next five years.
But analysts believe this will be an uphill struggle for the four-nation European consortium after Boeing completes its takeover of its smaller U.S. rival.
If Airbus had been more decisive it might have captured America's number two civil planemaker for itself, they said.
At the weekend Boeing Co announced it planned to take over McDonnell Douglas in a deal that would create a civil, and military giant with almost $50 billion in annual sales.

Analysts believe that most of McDonnell Douglas' civil jet transport output will gradually grind to a halt as orders are filled. Only the new MD-95, its smallest twin-jet carrying 100 passengers, and the MD-11 twin-jet freighter are seen to have a production future.
European airlines have 538 McDonnell Douglas planes in their fleets, according to data from Flight International, just under 20 per cent of the total of 2,701 jet aircraft.
Airbus must be hoping that when these planes are replaced it will have the inside track for these contracts on its home turf.
Alitalia, Iberia and its Aviaco subsidiary are the biggest operators of McDonnell Douglas aircraft. Scandinavian Airlines, Finnair, Austrian Airlines and Swissair are also big customers.

Richard Whitaker, editor of Airline Business Magazine, reckons that over the next five years about 160 McDonnell Douglas planes will be phased out, comprising 13 old DC-8s, 93 early DC-9s and 54 big DC-10 tri-jets.
"About 50 of those will cost $100 million each to replace, the other hundred about $30 million, which comes to about $8 billion," Whitaker said.
If Airbus is hoping to to win orders by playing the patriotic card in Europe, it is unlikely to make much headway.

"The bottom line is commercial realities. With the liberalisatiion of the European domestic market, we're looking at the evolution of a global airline business," said Chris Partridge, senior analyst with aviation consulting group Avmark.

"Cost is now the principle driver; Airbus might wish to address the nationalistic tendency, but they are not going to win with that one. Even Air France is taking the commercial route now," Partridge said.
Whitaker said Airbus had been negotiating to buy the commercial aeroplane division of McDonnell, especially after merger talks between the two U.S. companies broke down about a year ago.

"What a lost opportunity. They (Airbus) were the one company which could have been in a position to bid for McDonnell Douglas. If they'd done so they would have created a competitor roughly equal to Boeing. Now Boeing is going to be a great deal stronger than Airbus," Whitaker said.

Paul Beaver, spokesman for Jane's Defence Weekly agreed, and said Airbus would have been in a good position to challenge for future McDonnell replacement orders in Europe. Now the challenge of a combined McDonnell-Boeing might prove too strong.
"This is a blow for Airbus. They were hoping to get 50-50 with Boeing, but Boeing will now have 60 to 70 per cent of the (world) market with Airbus staying at about 35," Beaver said.
Airbus comprises Germany' Daimler Aerospace, Aerospatiale of France, British Aerospace and Spain's Construcciones Aeronauticas SA. Italian aerospace firm Alenia will also join in future projects.
